data.question: Should the operator keep the current rules (v1), given that block_k 3 → 2 again improves on-time deliveries but was voted down by B and C, and can be adopted only through a quorum change that both the operator (D2) and the regulator (R2) have declined?
data.background: Option 1 passed check and the constitution, but B and C voted against it, so it is blocked 1-2. The only route to adoption is a regulation revision, which D2 and R2 declined. Whether to reopen that route is a human decision about voting rights and third-party safety, not something I can settle. R2 left an open question: are the extra road violations harmless enforcement evictions? This measurement does not include a by-cause violation breakdown, and the gain held on only 3/5 seeds, so the human must judge whether the evidence now meets the bar R2 set.

options.summary: Tighten blocking_guard so a parked robot is evicted when 2 (not 3) robots wait behind it. Measured: on-time 213.6 → 219.4 (+5.8, 3/5 seeds improved), late 9.2 → 3.4, blocked s 1888 → 1217, lowest on-time rate 0.93 → 0.96, worst_company_p95_wait_s 154 → 95.4, unfinished 0.0 → 0.0. Road violations rise 24.2 → 34.8. Votes are A for, B and C against, so it cannot be adopted unless the quorum is revised, which the operator and regulator have declined.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain: more on-time deliveries, fewer late ones, a higher floor for the worst-served company, and shorter worst-case waits. A gains (utility 70.2 → 75.6). B loses (69.6 → 62.5). C loses the most (58.3 → 46.9, about 20%). Other road users carry an undiagnosed risk from about 45% more road violations. All three companies would lose their veto if this were forced through by a quorum change.

options.summary: No change; stay at v1. Measured: on-time 213.6, late 9.2, blocked s 1888, road violations 24.2, lowest on-time rate 0.93, worst_company_p95_wait_s 154, unfinished 0.0. The vote result (A for, B and C against) stands.
options.stakeholders: Customers forgo about 5.8 on-time deliveries and keep about 5.8 more late deliveries per period, and the worst-served company's customers wait longer (p95 154 vs 95.4). This is now the fourth period in which this cost is accepted. B and C keep their current utility (69.6 / 58.3). A forgoes its gain. Third parties avoid the extra road violations. Every company's veto and the current voting structure stay intact.

recommendation.reason: Option 1 is blocked by B's and C's votes, and the only override, a quorum change, was declined in D2 and R2 for reasons that still hold. The evidence is weaker than before: 3/5 seeds improved versus 5/5 in earlier periods. Road violations rise 24.2 → 34.8 with no by-cause breakdown in this measurement, so R2's open question remains unanswered. R2's own reconsideration condition (all KPI conditions on all seeds, no rise in road violations) is not met. C's utility loss (58.3 → 46.9) also remains unexplained. The next step is to measure the violation breakdown and why C and B lose, or to design a variant that B and C can accept, rather than reopening the regulation now.
assumptions: The table's road violations figure does not distinguish enforcement evictions from unsafe events.
B and C would vote against option 1 again if it were re-proposed unchanged.
The regulator's R2 conditions still describe what it would accept.
The 3/5 seed result reflects genuine variance rather than a measurement error.

Each company's policy and whether B or C would accept a modified block_k proposal.
How customers perceive the continuing late deliveries and longer waits across four periods.
Next period's demand and whether the size of the gain would hold.
